stem: What is the least number of distinct integers that must be chosen from {1,...,20} to guarantee two with sum 21?
optionRationales: Confuse a possible pair with a guaranteed pair.
Correct: Establish a sharp pigeonhole threshold.
Overestimate the pigeonhole threshold.
Give the largest size of a set avoiding the pair.
Assume every number must be selected.
solution: Partition the set into ten pairs (1,20),(2,19),...,(10,11), each summing to 21.
Eleven selections force two from one pair.
Ten are insufficient: {1,...,10} contains no such pair. The least threshold is eleven.
hints: Group numbers into complementary pairs.
Prove both a guarantee and a one-smaller counterexample.
misconception: Give the largest size of a set avoiding the pair.
decision: Establish a sharp pigeonhole threshold.

verification.method: Ten-pair partition and explicit size-ten avoiding set.

stem: What is the least number of distinct integers chosen from {1,...,30} that guarantees one selected integer divides another?
optionRationales: Correct: Invent a pigeonhole partition adapted to divisibility.
Assume all integers are needed.
Use too few groups based only on powers of two.
Group by ordinary remainders rather than divisibility chains.
Report the largest avoiding set rather than the forcing threshold.
solution: Write every integer uniquely as an odd number times a power of two.
The fifteen possible odd parts form fifteen chains in which the smaller number divides the larger. Sixteen selections force two from one chain.
The fifteen numbers 16 through 30 contain no divisibility pair, since doubling any exceeds 30. Thus sixteen is least.
hints: Remove all factors of two from each selected integer.
Numbers with the same odd part form a divisibility chain.
misconception: Report the largest avoiding set rather than the forcing threshold.
decision: Invent a pigeonhole partition adapted to divisibility.

verification.method: Unique odd-part chains and the explicit antichain 16 through 30.

stem: Two diagonally opposite corner squares are removed from an 8×8 chessboard. How many tilings of the remainder by 1×2 dominoes are possible?
optionRationales: Correct: Use a coloring invariant to prove impossibility.
Assume one tiling for each orientation.
Assume area divisibility guarantees a tiling.
Count remaining squares instead of tilings.
Report the number of dominoes rather than tilings.
solution: Color the board as a checkerboard. Every domino covers one square of each color.
Diagonally opposite corners have the same color, so the remaining board has thirty of one color and thirty-two of the other.
The unequal color counts make every domino tiling impossible. The answer is zero.
hints: Find a quantity every domino contributes equally.
Compare that quantity after the two removals.
misconception: Assume area divisibility guarantees a tiling.
decision: Use a coloring invariant to prove impossibility.

verification.method: Independent remaining-color count; the domino invariant proves nonexistence.

stem: Start with 1,2,3,4,5. Repeatedly replace any two numbers a,b by a+b+ab until one remains. What is that final number?
optionRationales: Use the product of the original numbers and then subtract one.
Correct: Discover a shifted-product invariant.
Forget to undo the final shift.
Assume the unshifted product is invariant.
Assume the sum is invariant.
solution: The replacement satisfies (a+b+ab)+1=(a+1)(b+1).
Thus the product of one more than every current number is invariant, initially 2·3·4·5·6=720.
When only N remains, N+1=720, so N=719 regardless of the choices.
hints: Add one to the replacement expression and factor it.
Look for a product preserved when two entries merge.
misconception: Assume the sum is invariant.
decision: Discover a shifted-product invariant.

stem: Three piles contain 10,11,12 stones. A move adds one stone to each of two piles and removes two from the third, provided no pile becomes negative. How many equal-pile configurations can be reached?
optionRationales: Report the total number of stones.
Choose which pile reaches the average first.
Use total-sum preservation as if it were sufficient.
Report the target size of each pile.
Correct: Combine two invariants to rule out a feasible-looking target.
solution: The total remains 33, so the only equal-pile candidate is (11,11,11).
Modulo three, every coordinate increases by one on every move, since -2≡1. Therefore pairwise differences modulo three are invariant.
The initial differences are not all zero modulo three, while the target differences are. The target is unreachable.
hints: The sum identifies a candidate but may not establish reachability.
Compare pairwise differences modulo three under one move.
misconception: Use total-sum preservation as if it were sufficient.
decision: Combine two invariants to rule out a feasible-looking target.

verification.method: Direct transition residue check; invariant separates start and target.

stem: Six players each play one game against every other player, with no draws. What is the largest possible number of players with at least four wins?
optionRationales: Ignore the total number of wins.
Find a bound but miss a cyclic equality construction.
Allow every player to win each mutual game.
Correct: Combine a global sum bound with a local cyclic construction.
Count potential strong players without accounting for their mutual games.
solution: There are C(6,2)=15 games and therefore fifteen wins. Four players with four wins would need sixteen, so at most three qualify.
Take three players who each beat the other three. Among the strong trio, arrange a cyclic win pattern so each wins one more.
All three then have four wins, proving the maximum is three.
hints: Every game contributes exactly one win to the total.
After obtaining a bound, construct a tournament that attains it.
misconception: Ignore the total number of wins.
decision: Combine a global sum bound with a local cyclic construction.

stem: What is the largest size of a subset of {1,...,12} containing no two consecutive integers?
optionRationales: Exceed the pair-partition bound.
Leave two unused integers between every selection.
Ignore the exclusion.
Correct: Pair an extremal upper bound with an explicit construction.
Miss an attainable endpoint selection.
solution: Partition into the six pairs {1,2},{3,4},...,{11,12}. At most one number from each pair can be chosen.
This gives an upper bound of six.
The odd numbers 1,3,5,7,9,11 attain it.
hints: Use disjoint pairs to obtain a bound.
Check an alternating set for equality.
misconception: Exceed the pair-partition bound.
decision: Pair an extremal upper bound with an explicit construction.

stem: What is the largest size of a subset of {1,...,25} in which no two distinct selected numbers have sum divisible by 6?
optionRationales: Ignore one of the self-complementary restrictions.
Correct: Optimize a residue-class packing with self-complementary cases.
Omit the extra member in residue class one.
Allow multiple numbers in self-complementary residue classes.
Discard both residue-zero and residue-three representatives unnecessarily.
solution: Classes 1 and 5 cannot both be represented; their sizes are five and four, so at most five can be taken from their union. Classes 2 and 4 similarly contribute at most four.
Within class zero, or within class three, any two distinct numbers have sum divisible by six, so each contributes at most one.
The bound is 5+4+1+1=11, attained by taking all residues 1 and 2 plus one number from each of classes 0 and 3.
hints: Pair complementary residue classes.
Residues zero and three are their own complements and need different treatment.
misconception: Allow multiple numbers in self-complementary residue classes.
decision: Optimize a residue-class packing with self-complementary cases.

verification.method: Independent class counts and explicit eleven-element witness.

stem: Six coins lie in a row, initially all heads. A move flips two adjacent coins. How many configurations are reachable?
optionRationales: Impose an extra unsupported invariant.
Ignore the parity invariant.
Count only one-move configurations and the start.
Correct: Prove both necessity and sufficiency of a parity invariant.
Exclude the initial configuration.
solution: Every move preserves the parity of the number of tails, so at most 2^5=32 configurations are reachable.
For any desired even-tail configuration, scan from left to right. Whenever a position is wrong, flip it with the next coin, fixing it permanently.
After the first five positions are fixed, parity forces the last to be correct. Thus every even-tail configuration is reachable.
hints: Find an invariant first.
Then give a procedure reaching every configuration that satisfies it.
misconception: Ignore the parity invariant.
decision: Prove both necessity and sufficiency of a parity invariant.

stem: What is the least number of people guaranteeing that among them are either three mutual acquaintances or three mutual strangers, assuming acquaintance is symmetric?
optionRationales: Correct: Combine a local pigeonhole argument with a graph construction.
Omit the five-cycle counterexample.
Use a nonsharp guarantee.
Assume any three people are homogeneous.
Apply the pigeonhole principle one stage too early.
solution: With six people, choose one person. At least three of the other five have the same acquaintance relation to that person.
If any two of those three share that relation, they form a homogeneous triple with the chosen person; otherwise the three themselves form a triple of the opposite relation.
Five people can avoid both: make acquaintance edges a five-cycle. Neither it nor its complement contains a triangle. Thus six is least.
hints: Focus on the relations from one chosen person.
For sharpness, search for a symmetric five-person counterexample.
misconception: Omit the five-cycle counterexample.
decision: Combine a local pigeonhole argument with a graph construction.

verification.method: Exhaustive two-color graphs through six vertices; proof certificate: three same-colored incident edges force a monochromatic triangle; a five-cycle and its complement are triangle-free.

stem: Distinct positive integers have sum 10. What is the largest possible product?
optionRationales: Use 1,2,3,4 without comparing three-part choices.
Use the repeated parts 3,3,4, violating distinctness.
Use 2,4,5, whose sum exceeds ten.
Use three equal threes, violating distinctness and the sum.
Correct: Respect distinctness while proving a product maximum.
solution: At most four distinct positive integers can be used because 1+2+3+4+5>10. Four force the set {1,2,3,4}, with product 24.
For three integers a<b<c, listing a=1 or 2 gives maximum 20 or 30, and a=3 is impossible because 3+4+5>10.
The largest triple is {2,3,5}, with product 30; compare two-part products, whose maximum is 4·6=24.
hints: Bound the number of parts using the smallest distinct integers.

misconception: Use 1,2,3,4 without comparing three-part choices.

stem: Start with the integers 1 through 10. Repeatedly replace two current numbers by their absolute difference until one remains. What is the largest possible final number?
optionRationales: Assume all merge orders lead to the same result.
Use only the maximum bound and ignore parity.
Correct: Combine a monotone bound, an invariant, and an attaining construction.
Assume the sum can survive subtraction.
Ignore the odd total-sum invariant.
solution: No operation increases the largest entry, so the final number is at most ten. Replacing a,b by |a-b| changes the sum by an even number, so its final parity is that of 55: odd.
Thus the upper bound is nine. To attain it, pair 9 with 8, 7 with 6, 5 with 4, and 3 with 2, leaving five ones and ten.
Cancel pairs of ones to zero and absorb the zeros, leaving one and ten; their difference is nine.
hints: Track both the largest entry and the sum modulo two.
A bound is not enough: exhibit a sequence reaching it.
misconception: Use only the maximum bound and ignore parity.

stem: Start with (84,30). Repeatedly subtract the smaller positive entry from the larger until the entries are equal. What is their final sum?

stem: The numbers 1 through 10 are arranged around a circle. What is the least possible value of the largest sum of two adjacent numbers?
optionRationales: Use the average bound without checking whether equality is possible.

Equal adjacent sums would force every second entry to repeat, impossible with ten distinct numbers. Thus the largest sum is at least twelve.
The arrangement 1,10,2,9,3,8,4,7,5,6 has every adjacent sum at most twelve, so twelve is attainable.
hints: Average all adjacent sums to obtain a lower bound.

stem: Positive real numbers x,y have sum 10. What is the largest possible xy?
optionRationales: Square the sum without cross-term accounting.
Correct: Prove and attain a fixed-sum product bound.

Use twice the maximum product.
Choose an unbalanced pair.

Equality is attained at x=y=5, which satisfies the domain.

stem: Positive real numbers x,y,z satisfy x+y+z=12. What is the least possible $1/x+1/y+1/z$?
optionRationales: Use the reciprocal of the total.
Keep only one of the three equal reciprocal terms.
Assume integer variables must be unequal.
Correct: Match an inequality to a reciprocal target and verify equality.
Double the sharp lower bound.
solution: Cauchy–Schwarz gives (x+y+z)(1/x+1/y+1/z)≥(1+1+1)²=9.
The reciprocal sum is therefore at least 9/12=3/4.
Equality requires x=y=z=4 and is feasible, proving the minimum.

Determine whether equality is compatible with the sum constraint.

stem: For x>0, what is the least possible value of $x+9/x$?
optionRationales: Use the geometric mean without its factor two.
Choose x=1 without proving it is best.
Correct: Use a constant-product sum bound.
Ignore positivity and the reciprocal constraint.
Optimize only one term.
solution: AM–GM gives x+9/x≥2√9=6.
Equality requires x=9/x, hence x=3 in the positive domain.
The value six is attained there.
hints: The product of the two terms is constant.
Solve the equality condition using the stated sign restriction.
misconception: Use the geometric mean without its factor two.

stem: Positive real numbers x,y satisfy x+y=1. What is the largest possible $xy^2$?
optionRationales: Forget the factor four after splitting y.
Assume x=y without accounting for the repeated y factor.
Maximize xy and then ignore the extra y.
Correct: Choose weighted equality proportions rather than assuming symmetry.
Lose one of the two half-y factors.

AM–GM gives x(y/2)²≤(1/3)³, so xy²≤4/27.
Equality occurs at x=1/3,y=2/3, which meets the original constraint.

Apply a three-term inequality with a fixed sum.
misconception: Assume x=y without accounting for the repeated y factor.

stem: Positive real numbers x,y,z satisfy x+y+z=15 and $(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)=8xyz$. Find $x^2+y^2+z^2$.
optionRationales: Use the squared sum without subtracting cross terms.

Correct: Extract a unique configuration from simultaneous equality cases.
solution: Each factor obeys x+y≥2√(xy), and similarly for the other two.
The product is at least 8xyz. The given equality forces equality in all three positive-factor inequalities, so x=y=z.
The sum makes each variable five; the requested sum of squares is 75.
hints: Compare each factor with twice the geometric mean of its terms.
Equality of the positive product forces every individual lower bound to be tight.
misconception: Use the squared sum without subtracting cross terms.

stem: For real x for which it is defined, what is the greatest value of $\sqrt{x+5}+\sqrt{5-x}$?
optionRationales: Correct: Use a domain-safe square to expose a maximum.
Double-count the two terms after squaring.
Keep only one radical at the equality point x=0.
Use the radicands rather than their square roots.
Combine square roots by adding radicands.
solution: The domain is -5≤x≤5. Squaring the nonnegative expression gives 10+2√(25-x²).
This is at most 20 because x²≥0.
The maximum is √20=2√5, attained at x=0.

stem: Find the sum of all real solutions of $\sqrt{x+6}=x$.
optionRationales: Correct: Reject extraneous roots introduced by squaring.

stem: What is the product of the real solutions of $|x-2|+|x+4|=10$?
optionRationales: Lose the sign of the negative solution.

Report the constant minimum distance.

For x≥2 the equation is 2x+2=10, giving x=4. For x≤-4 it is -2x-2=10, giving x=-6.
The product is 4(-6)=-24. Both candidates lie in their assumed intervals.
hints: Split the line at the two absolute-value breakpoints.

stem: The set of real x satisfying $\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor2x\rfloor=10$ is an interval. What is its length?
optionRationales: Assume only an integer solution is possible.
Correct: Reduce a floor equation to a finite residue choice and an interval.
Treat both floors as constant across a full unit interval.
Replace the floor sum by floor(3x).
Double the interval instead of halving it.
solution: Write x=n+f with integer n and 0≤f<1. The equation becomes 3n+floor(2f)=10.
The last floor is zero or one, so n=3 and floor(2f)=1.
Thus 1/2≤f<1, giving x in [7/2,4), of length 1/2.
hints: Separate integer and fractional parts.
The doubled fractional part has only two possible floor values.
misconception: Treat both floors as constant across a full unit interval.
decision: Reduce a floor equation to a finite residue choice and an interval.

verification.method: Independent rational-grid interval check; exact endpoint proof establishes the continuous interval.

stem: For how many integers k with 0≤k≤30 does $\lfloor k/10\rfloor+\lfloor1-k/10\rfloor=0$?
optionRationales: Miss one endpoint with integer input.

stem: For how many integers k with 1≤k≤10 does $t^2-2kt+k+2$ have two distinct positive real roots?
optionRationales: Include the repeated-root case k=2.

Correct: Combine a domain condition with coefficient-based root signs.

stem: Positive integers x,y,z satisfy x+y+z=11. What is the largest possible xyz?

stem: For x>0, $\log_2x\,\log_4x\,\log_8x=36$. Find x.
optionRationales: Use an exponent one below the solution.

Treat the product of bases as the base of one logarithm.
Report the transformed logarithm.
solution: With t=log₂x, the product is t·(t/2)·(t/3)=t³/6.
Thus t³=216 and the unique real t is six.
Therefore x=2⁶=64.

stem: Find the sum of all real solutions of $4^x-5\cdot2^x+4=0$.

stem: How many integers x satisfy $\log_{1/2}(x-1)>-2$?

stem: For $0<\theta<\pi/2$, $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt{3/2}$. Find $\tan\theta+\cot\theta$.
optionRationales: Correct: Connect a symmetric trigonometric sum to a rational target.
Report sinθ cosθ instead of its reciprocal.
Report the squared given value.
Omit the factor two in the squared sum.

Combining the target fractions gives (sin²θ+cos²θ)/(sinθ cosθ).

Compute cos²θ instead.
Compute sin²θ instead.

solution: On the unit circle, z^-1 is the conjugate, so Re(z)=√3/2.
The two possibilities are z=√3/2±i/2, with arguments ±π/6.
Their sixth powers and inverse sixth powers are both -1, giving -2.
hints: Use the unit-modulus condition to interpret the reciprocal.
Determine the possible arguments before taking powers.
misconception: Use a full-turn angle instead of a half-turn.
decision: Combine conjugation, unit-circle geometry, and a power.

stem: What is the sum of the four fifth roots of unity other than 1?
optionRationales: Assume each nontrivial root has real part minus one.
Forget to subtract the omitted root.
Correct: Use Vieta to evaluate a symmetric complex sum.
Use the sum of all five roots.
Add moduli instead of complex numbers.
solution: The sum of all roots of z^5-1 is zero by its z⁴ coefficient.
One root is one.
The other four therefore sum to -1.
hints: Use a polynomial coefficient to sum all roots.
Remove the omitted root only after summing the full set.
misconception: Use the sum of all five roots.
decision: Use Vieta to evaluate a symmetric complex sum.

verification.method: Independent Vieta on the nontrivial-root polynomial.

stem: Let $\zeta_0,\ldots,\zeta_4$ be all fifth roots of unity. Find $\prod_{k=0}^{4}(2-\zeta_k)$.
optionRationales: Omit the constant term of the root polynomial.
Reverse all five factors without changing the sign.
Correct: Evaluate a symmetric root product directly.
Use the wrong number of roots.
Use z^5+1 instead of z^5-1.
solution: The monic polynomial with these roots is t^5-1.
Its root factorization is the requested product when evaluated at t=2.
The result is 2^5-1=31. No individual roots need to be calculated.
hints: Recognize a product over every root of one polynomial.
Evaluate that polynomial at the common shift.
misconception: Omit the constant term of the root polynomial.
decision: Evaluate a symmetric root product directly.

stem: Let ζ run over the six seventh roots of unity other than 1. Find $\sum 1/(1-\zeta)$.
optionRationales: Report the average contribution rather than the sum.
Count one for every root instead of every inverse pair.
Correct: Use inverse-pair cancellation on a rational root sum.
Assume the reciprocal sum inherits the ordinary root sum.
Reverse every denominator.
solution: The nontrivial roots pair as ζ and ζ^-1, with no root equal to its own inverse.
For each pair, $1/(1-\zeta)+1/(1-\zeta^{-1})=1$, obtained by combining fractions.
There are three pairs, so the sum is three. None of the denominators vanishes.
hints: Pair roots with their reciprocals.
Simplify one pair before summing all six terms.
misconception: Count one for every root instead of every inverse pair.
decision: Use inverse-pair cancellation on a rational root sum.

stem: How many solutions of $z^{12}=1$ have strictly positive real part?
optionRationales: Include both imaginary-axis roots.
Exclude the positive real root one.
Use positive modulus instead of positive real part.
Correct: Count roots in a strict angular region.
Include one of the imaginary-axis boundary roots.
solution: The twelve roots have arguments kπ/6 for k=0,...,11.
Positive real part means cos(kπ/6)>0, selecting k=0,1,2,10,11.
There are five; k=3 and 9 lie on the imaginary axis and are excluded.
hints: Place the roots at equally spaced angles on the unit circle.
Treat roots on the boundary separately from roots in the open half-plane.
misconception: Include one of the imaginary-axis boundary roots.
decision: Count roots in a strict angular region.

stem: Complex numbers z satisfy $|z-1|=|z+1|$ and $|z-2i|=\sqrt5$. Find the product of all such z.
optionRationales: Use the sum of the imaginary coordinates as a product.
Confuse the center sum with the product.
Correct: Translate complex-distance conditions into intersecting loci.
Use the circle radius squared.
Forget that i²=-1 when multiplying the imaginary coordinates.
solution: The first locus is the perpendicular bisector of -1 and 1, so z=iy for real y.
The second condition gives (y-2)²=5, hence y=2±√5.
The product of the two z values is i²(4-5)=1.
hints: Interpret each modulus equation as a geometric locus.
Intersect the imaginary axis with the given circle.
misconception: Forget that i²=-1 when multiplying the imaginary coordinates.
decision: Translate complex-distance conditions into intersecting loci.

verification.method: Exact circle-line roots substituted and multiplied.

stem: The point represented by 1+i is rotated 90° counterclockwise about the point 2+i. What complex number represents its image?
optionRationales: Reflect across the center instead of quarter-turning.
Correct: Compose translation and complex multiplication.
Rotate about the origin instead of the stated center.
Translate without the correct rotation.
Rotate clockwise instead.
solution: Subtract the center: (1+i)-(2+i)=-1.
Multiply the displacement by i for a counterclockwise quarter-turn, giving -i.
Add the center back: 2+i-i=2.
hints: Translate the rotation center to zero.
Multiply the displacement by i, then restore the center.
misconception: Rotate clockwise instead.
decision: Compose translation and complex multiplication.

stem: The first two consecutive vertices of a square, listed counterclockwise, are 1+2i and 4+6i. What is the squared modulus of its center?
optionRationales: Use the midpoint of the given side as the square center.
Forget to average opposite vertices.
Correct: Use orientation-sensitive complex geometry.
Use the square on the opposite side of the directed edge.
Report the side length squared.
solution: The directed edge is 3+4i. Turning it counterclockwise gives i(3+4i)=-4+3i.
The third vertex is (4+6i)+(-4+3i)=9i, so the center is the midpoint of 1+2i and 9i: 1/2+(11/2)i.
Its squared modulus is 1/4+121/4=61/2. The orientation selects one of two possible squares.
hints: Use multiplication by i to obtain the next directed edge.
The center is the midpoint of opposite, not adjacent, vertices.
misconception: Report the side length squared.
decision: Use orientation-sensitive complex geometry.

stem: Evaluate $(1+i)^{20}$.
optionRationales: Correct: Apply polar powers with independent magnitude and angle tracking.
Assume powers cancel because the real and imaginary parts begin equal.
Use modulus √2 without raising it through all twenty powers.
Use an argument one quarter-turn away.
Ignore the final argument.
solution: Write 1+i=√2(cos(π/4)+i sin(π/4)).
The twentieth power has modulus (√2)^20=1024 and argument 5π.
Since cos5π=-1 and sin5π=0, the value is -1024.
hints: Separate modulus from argument.
Reduce the multiplied argument modulo a full turn.
misconception: Ignore the final argument.
decision: Apply polar powers with independent magnitude and angle tracking.

stem: Find $\binom{12}0+\binom{12}4+\binom{12}8+\binom{12}{12}$.
optionRationales: Sum the entire binomial row.
Assume the four residue classes have exactly equal coefficient sums.
Use the wrong sign for the imaginary evaluations.
Filter only parity rather than residue modulo four.
Correct: Use a roots-of-unity filter for a coefficient residue class.
solution: For P(t)=(1+t)^12, the average [P(1)+P(-1)+P(i)+P(-i)]/4 retains exactly exponents divisible by four.
These values are 4096,0,-64,-64.
The sum is (4096-128)/4=992. The complex terms correct the tempting equal-quarter estimate.
hints: Evaluate at the fourth roots of unity to filter exponents.
Averaging cancels powers whose exponent is not divisible by four.
misconception: Assume the four residue classes have exactly equal coefficient sums.
decision: Use a roots-of-unity filter for a coefficient residue class.

stem: A walk starts at 0 in the complex plane. Each of ten steps adds one of 1,-1,i,-i. How many step sequences return to 0?
optionRationales: Count only one horizontal-vertical balance split.
Correct: Connect complex displacement to a balanced-word identity.
Count all walks.
Identify a walk with its reversal.
Choose only the positions of one direction without assigning all four.
solution: A returning walk has k east and k west steps, and 5-k north and 5-k south steps.
For fixed k, the count is 10!/[k!²(5-k)!²]=C(10,5)C(5,k)².
Sum over k and use Vandermonde: C(10,5)·C(10,5)=252²=63504.
hints: Return to zero requires separate horizontal and vertical balance.
Partition by the number of steps in one horizontal direction.
misconception: Choose only the positions of one direction without assigning all four.
decision: Connect complex displacement to a balanced-word identity.

verification.method: Independent dynamic programming on integer coordinate displacements.

stem: A regular heptagon is inscribed in the unit circle. From one vertex, sum the squares of the distances to the other six vertices.
optionRationales: Assume the other six roots sum to zero.
Correct: Combine a norm identity with a symmetric root sum.
Double every chord-square contribution.
Omit the cross-term contribution of the other roots.
Add unit radii instead of chord lengths.
solution: Rotate the chosen vertex to 1. For another unit root ζ, |1-ζ|²=2-ζ-conjugate(ζ).
The six other roots sum to -1, and their conjugates also sum to -1.
The total is 12-(-1)-(-1)=14. This avoids calculating six individual chord lengths.
hints: Express a chord length squared using conjugation.
Sum the roots before evaluating individual angles.
misconception: Omit the cross-term contribution of the other roots.
decision: Combine a norm identity with a symmetric root sum.

verification.method: Independent numerical chord-square sum supports the exact root-sum proof.

stem: A regular heptagon is inscribed in the unit circle. From one vertex, multiply the distances to all other vertices. What is the product?
optionRationales: Use the squared-distance sum identity instead.
Correct: Convert a geometric product into a polynomial value.
Add the number of distances instead of multiplying.
Report the square of the product.
Assume unit radii imply unit chords.
solution: Let the chosen vertex be 1 and the other roots be ζ. The polynomial with those six roots is Q(t)=(t^7-1)/(t-1)=1+t+...+t^6.
Evaluating at t=1 gives product(1-ζ)=Q(1)=7.
Taking absolute values changes the complex product into the requested product of chord lengths, still seven.
hints: Remove the known root from the seventh-root polynomial.
Evaluate the remaining root product at the chosen vertex, then take moduli.
misconception: Assume unit radii imply unit chords.
decision: Convert a geometric product into a polynomial value.

verification.method: Independent numerical product of exact chord formulas supports the polynomial proof.
